newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibia central bank sees better growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Namibia central bank sees better growth in 1997.

text.p: Namibia's central bank expects economic growth of three to four percent in 1997 compared with a little under three percent in 1996, because of improvements in mining, agriculture and fishing.

Central bank governor Tom Alweendo told Reuters in an interview: "The main prospect of growth is probably still with the mining industry and hopefully also the fishing sector. What we hear is that the fish stock is recovering for 1997," he said.
"We also just had some good rains and that is going to be a relief, especially for the agricultural sector."
Inflation will stabilise, according to Alweendo, who points out that the rate of inflation has been on a downward trend over the last three years.
"For 1996 it stood at about 8.5 percent, and we're predicting that it won't exceed that figure in 1997."

The central bank is not unduly concerned about the current level of government borrowing. Figures released recently by the Namibian Economic Policy Research Unit showed Namibia's debt had increased from N$731 million ($159 million) to N$1.9 billion since independence in 1990.

"We're quite confident that it won't put too much pressure on the inflation figure, because most of the borrowing as relating to the budget goes into development and doesn't go all into consumption," said Alweendo.
"One should not be complacent of course, and there has been an increase, but the level of borrowing at 1990 figures was really barely anything."
In comparison with other Southern African Development Community (SADC) countries Namibia still had very low debts, he added.

Interest rates are currently high in Namibia, with the Bank of Namibia's lending rate to the commercial banks at 17.5 percent -- primarily because of the Namibian dollar's one-for-one link to the South African rand.
"The Namibian interest rate is really mainly reflecting what's happening in South Africa and the whole of 1996 there has seen a lot of turbulence in the foreign exchange markets.
"But the indications are that the exchange rate is stabilizing now and we hope that this will be a permanent trend."

Alweendo said he saw no prospect of a delinking of the Namibian currency in the near future. The link made sense because Namibia imports most of its goods from South Africa, and because both economies are so similar, Alweendo said.
Namibia's Export Processing Zone should provide additional stimulus to the economy going forward, he said.
"Depending on the success of the ones already operating, you could say by the end of this year there might be more companies putting up their factories." ($=4.58 Namibian dollars)
